title: Meat Burrito with Rice, No Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A meat burrito with rice, no cheese is a Mexican dish consisting of a large flour tortilla filled with seasoned meat, cooked rice, beans, vegetables and sauces, but without cheese. The tortilla is often lightly toasted, giving it a soft yet slightly crisp texture, while the filling makes the meal hearty and nutritious.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico in the early 20th century as a portable meal for workers.
While the original burrito featured only beans and rice, meat has become one of the most popular fillings today.
Leaving out cheese makes the dish suitable for people with lactose intolerance.
Tortillas are frequently made from whole‑wheat flour, increasing fiber content.
Burritos are commonly served with guacamole, salsa, and sour cream, but lighter sauces can be used as alternatives.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: The meat provides a complete set of essential amino acids needed for muscle repair and metabolic functions.

items.title: Energy‑rich rice
items.content: Cooked rice supplies complex carbohydrates that deliver sustained energy and keep you full longer.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain tortillas contain B1, B3, and B6 vitamins, supporting nervous system health.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Rice, beans, and vegetables add dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: Omitting cheese eliminates lactose, making the burrito safe for those with lactose sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium levels
items.content: Sauces and marinades can add a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with high blood pressure.

items.title: Fat content of meat
items.content: Using fatty cuts increases calories and may not fit low‑fat diet plans.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure it is cooked thoroughly.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional flour tortillas contain gluten, so the dish is unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are convenient to eat by hand, but you can also cut them in half and add fresh veggies, guacamole, or salsa. For a lighter version, choose a whole‑grain or gluten‑free tortilla and lean meat such as turkey or trimmed beef.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. For freezing, wrap tightly in plastic film and keep in the freezer for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to ensure the filling is evenly hot.
